chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

"If the woman says to her husband in a general statement: 'I will not obey you in a specific or unspecified matter,' it becomes permissible for him to take (her dowry/mahr) from her, and he has no right of return (raj'ah) over her."

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The view I rely on in this chapter and issue fatwa based on is that the woman who performs khul' (redemption) must necessarily be followed by a divorce. This is the opinion of Ja'far ibn Sam'ah, al-Hasan ibn Sam'ah, Ali ibn Ribat, and Ibn Hudhayfah among the early scholars, and the opinion of Ali ibn al-Husayn among the later scholars. As for the rest of the early jurists of our school, I do not know of them issuing a fatwa to act upon it, and more than the narrations we mentioned and similar ones have not been transmitted from them. It is permissible that they narrated it in the manner we will mention later, even if their fatwa and practice were according to what we said. And that which indicates what we have gone to is what was narrated:

key_terms.رَجْعَة: Raj'ah (right of return/reconciliation without new contract)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal consequence when a wife declares she will not obey her husband in the context of khul?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the legal consequences of a wife’s general declaration of non-obedience, establishing the husband’s right to retain the dowry and effect a final divorce without revocation (*raj'ah*). Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Furaykati emphasizes that a formal divorce must follow this *khul'* to be valid, a position supported by key early and late Shia jurists like Ja'far ibn Sam'an and Ali ibn Hubayra, distinguishing their view from other scholars whose specific rulings on this matter were not explicitly recorded.
